abstract.para: Carry an existing &rmt; server across the distribution upgrade from &sle; 15 SP7 to &productname; &productnumber;, and repair the two platform changes that leave &rmt; unavailable afterwards.

topic.para: Upgrade the host itself with the distribution migration system, as described in Upgrading to &productname; &productnumber;. This section covers only the steps that are specific to a host running &rmt;.

important.title: A successful upgrade can still leave &rmt; unavailable
important.para: The distribution migration system reports success for the distribution upgrade, not for the services running on the host. Even when every suse-migration-* unit finishes with Result=success and /var/log/distro_migration.exitcode contains 0, &rmt; does not start until you complete the steps below.

step.para: Back up the &rmt; configuration file and the &rmt; database to a location outside the host:
Record the ownership of the &mariadb; data directory. On &sle; 15 it belongs to the group root, which is what breaks &mariadb; after the upgrade:

note.title: Registered clients follow the &rmt; server address
note.para: The upgrade replaces wicked with &nm;, which changes the DHCP client identifier. A host using DHCP is therefore likely to receive a different address. Clients registered against this &rmt; server reach it through the URL stored in their &zypper; service definitions, so assign the server a stable address or host name before you upgrade.

step.para: Check which services are running. &rmt; depends on &mariadb; through Requires=mariadb.service, so a failed database keeps &rmt; inactive:
Correct the group ownership of the &mariadb; data directory:

On &productname; &productnumber;, mariadb.service combines StateDirectory=mysql with User=mysql and Group=mysql. systemd therefore adjusts the ownership of /var/lib/mysql on every start, and the mysql:root ownership inherited from &sle; 15 makes that fail:
step.screen: mariadb.service: Failed to set up special execution directory in /var/lib: Permission denied mariadb.service: Control process exited, code=exited, status=238/STATE_DIRECTORY
step.para: The error is reported as a permission problem rather than an ownership one, which makes it easy to mistake for a file system or &selnx; fault.
Allow nginx to connect to the &rmt; back-end:

&productname; &productnumber; uses &selnx; in enforcing mode instead of AppArmor. The httpd_can_network_connect boolean is off by default, which prevents nginx from opening a connection to the &rmt; back-end on 127.0.0.1:4224. Without this setting, nginx answers every request that it proxies to &rmt; with 502.
401 is the expected answer on the registration endpoint: it shows that the &rmt; application is reachable and requires authentication. A 502 means that the previous step is incomplete.

Restart the host and repeat the checks. Confirming the result across a reboot matters here, because the &selnx; boolean only persists when it is set with -P, and because &mariadb; is often not enabled in its own right: rmt-server.service pulls it in through Requires=.

note.title: &rmt; 2 is upgraded to &rmt; 3
note.para: &sle; 15 SP7 offers both &rmt; 2 and &rmt; 3, while &productname; &productnumber; ships only &rmt; 3. A host still running &rmt; 2 therefore moves to &rmt; 3 as part of the distribution upgrade.

No action is required. /etc/rmt.conf and the contents of the database are preserved, and rmt-server-migration.service updates the database schema before rmt-server.service starts. &rmt; 3 differs from &rmt; 2 in the Ruby and Rails versions it runs on, not in its configuration file or its rmt-cli commands.

warning.title: Mirrored repositories keep working while registration is broken
warning.para: nginx serves /repo/ directly from disk, so clients continue to download packages even when the &rmt; application is unreachable and no client can register. Check the registration endpoint, not just the repository paths.
